title: NEB Class 11 Biology — Floral Diversity — 2024
subject: biology
source: NEB Grade 11 Model Questions / NEB Past Papers 2020-2024

questions.question: Classify the five kingdoms of living organisms. Give one characteristic feature of each.
questions.solution: **Monera** — prokaryotic, unicellular (bacteria). **Protista** — eukaryotic, mostly unicellular (algae, amoeba). **Fungi** — heterotrophic, chitin walls (mushrooms). **Plantae** — autotrophic, cellulose walls (mosses to angiosperms). **Animalia** — heterotrophic, no walls (sponges to mammals).
questions.answer: **Five kingdoms (Whittaker, 1969), one feature each:** **(1) Monera** — prokaryotes, no true nucleus (bacteria, cyanobacteria); **(2) Protista** — unicellular eukaryotes with true nucleus (*Amoeba*, *Paramecium*); **(3) Fungi** — absorptive heterotrophs with chitinous cell walls and hyphal bodies (mushroom, *Mucor*); **(4) Plantae** — multicellular photosynthetic autotrophs with cellulose walls (moss, fern, mango); **(5) Animalia** — multicellular ingestive heterotrophs without cell walls, most with nervous coordination (frog, man). **Deep point:** the classification's blade is nutrition — make food (plants), absorb food (fungi), swallow food (animals) — with prokaryote/eukaryote and unicellular/multicellular as the other two cuts.

questions.question: Describe the general characteristics of the phylum Bryophyta. Give two economic importances.
questions.solution:
Small non-vascular plants; dominant gametophyte; need water for fertilisation; thalloid or leafy (Marchantia, Funaria).

**Importance:** Sphagnum peat (fuel, packing, seedbeds); ornamentals and traditional medicine.
questions.knowledgeNote: 'Amphibians of the plant kingdom' — tied to water for reproduction.
questions.answer: **Bryophyta characteristics:** non-vascular plants without true roots/stems/leaves (rhizoids only); gametophyte-dominant life cycle with dependent sporophyte; archegonia and antheridia as sex organs; **biflagellate sperm require water** for fertilisation (hence 'amphibians of the plant kingdom'); live in moist shady habitats; examples *Marchantia*, *Funaria*, *Sphagnum*. **Two economic importances:** (1) *Sphagnum* **peat** as fuel, packing material for live plants and antiseptic dressing; (2) **soil building and moisture retention** — pioneer colonisers of bare rock that prevent erosion (also used as beddings). **Deep point:** 'amphibian' is the key word — bryophytes live on land but still must marry in water, and every feature follows from that constraint.

questions.question: Distinguish between gymnosperms and angiosperms with two examples of each.
questions.solution:
**Gymnosperms:** naked seeds on cones, no flowers/fruits — e.g. *Pinus*, *Cycas*. Mostly evergreen, wind-pollinated.

**Angiosperms:** seeds enclosed in fruits, true flowers — e.g. rice, mustard. Dominant, insect/wind pollinated, double fertilisation.
questions.knowledgeNote: Double fertilisation (embryo + triploid endosperm) is the angiosperm-exclusive signature.
questions.answer: **Gymnosperms vs angiosperms:** **Seeds:** gymnosperms bear **naked seeds** on megasporophylls/cone scales — no ovary, so no fruit; angiosperms have **seeds enclosed in an ovary that matures into a fruit**. **Flowers:** gymnosperms have **cones (strobili)**, no true flowers; angiosperms have **true flowers** with carpels. **Xylem:** gymnosperm wood lacks vessels (tracheids only); angiosperms have **vessels** (more efficient water transport). **Fertilisation/pollination:** gymnosperms — wind pollination, pollen lands directly on the ovule; angiosperms — pollination to stigma, pollen tube grows through stylar tissue, double fertilisation forms endosperm. **Examples:** gymnosperms — **Pinus (pine), Cycas, Ginkgo**; angiosperms — **mango, wheat, mustard, orchid**. **Deep point:** 'naked vs enclosed seed' is the name's literal meaning (gymno = naked, angio = vessel) — the ovary's enclosure is the angiosperm's single most consequential innovation, protecting the seed and co-opting animals as pollinators and dispersers.

questions.question: Write the general characteristics of Pteridophyta with two examples.
questions.solution: First true land plants with **vascular tissue** (xylem, phloem); dominant **sporophyte**; reproduce by spores (seedless vascular plants); need water for fertilisation. Examples: *Dryopteris* (fern), *Equisetum* (horsetail).
questions.knowledgeNote: 'Reptiles of the plant kingdom' — first vascular, still water-bound for sex.
questions.answer: **Pteridophyta — general characteristics:** (1) **first true vascular plants** — xylem and phloem present, with true roots, stems and leaves; (2) **spore-producing** — sporangia in **sori** on the leaves (sporophylls); no seeds, no flowers; (3) **dominant independent sporophyte** with a small free-living gametophyte (prothallus); (4) **motile antherozoids need water** for fertilisation (like bryophytes — still tied to moisture); (5) alternation of generations, sporophyte photosynthetic and long-lived. **Examples:** ***Dryopteris*** (fern), ***Pteris***, *Selaginella*, *Equisetum* (horsetail), *Lycopodium*. **Deep point:** pteridophytes are the halfway house of plant evolution — vascular tissue like seed plants, but reproduction still water-dependent like bryophytes; coal is largely their ancient relatives.

questions.question: Classify algae into three major classes on the basis of pigments, with one example of each.
questions.solution:
**Chlorophyceae** (green — chlorophyll a/b): *Spirogyra*. **Phaeophyceae** (brown — fucoxanthin): *Sargassum*. **Rhodophyceae** (red — phycoerythrin): *Gracilaria*.

Pigment decides depth zones: red algae photosynthesise deepest.
questions.knowledgeNote: Agar (culture medium) and carrageenan (food gel) both come from red algae.
questions.answer: **Three classes of algae by pigments:** **(1) Chlorophyceae (green algae)** — pigments **chlorophyll a and b** dominate; stores starch; cell wall cellulose; e.g. ***Chlamydomonas***, *Spirogyra*, *Volvox*. **(2) Phaeophyceae (brown algae)** — pigment **fucoxanthin** (brown) masks chlorophylls; stores mannitol/laminarin; mostly marine, large (kelps); e.g. ***Laminaria***, *Sargassum*, *Fucus*. **(3) Rhodophyceae (red algae)** — pigment **r-phycoerythrin** (red) dominates; stores floridean starch; mostly marine, deep-water (red light penetrates deepest); e.g. ***Polysiphonia***, *Gelidium* (agar), *Porphyra* (nori). **Deep point:** the class colour *is* the pigment — the accessory pigments are evolutionary solutions to harvesting light at different depths, which is why red algae own the deepest zone.

questions.question: Write the general characteristics of fungi. Give one beneficial and one harmful example.
questions.solution:
Eukaryotic heterotrophs with **chitin** walls; absorptive nutrition; reproduce by spores; body of hyphae (mycelium).

Beneficial: *Penicillium* (antibiotics). Harmful: *Puccinia* (wheat rust).
questions.knowledgeNote: Lichens (fungus + alga) are the symbiotic showcase — two kingdoms, one body.
questions.answer: **General characteristics of fungi:** (1) **heterotrophic by absorption** — secrete digestive enzymes onto dead or living matter and absorb the products (saprophytic, parasitic or symbiotic); (2) body a **mycelium of thread-like hyphae**, often multinucleate and coenocytic; (3) cell wall of **chitin** (not cellulose); (4) **stored food is glycogen** (like animals, not starch); (5) reproduce by **spores** (and by budding/yeast, conjugation/*Mucor*); (6) non-motile, eukaryotic, prefer warm humid conditions. **One beneficial example:** ***Penicillium*** — source of the antibiotic penicillin (also yeast in bread/brewing, mushrooms as food). **One harmful example:** ***Puccinia*** (rust fungus) — destroys wheat crops (also *Phytophthora* late blight of potato, ringworm fungi on skin). **Deep point:** fungi are outside- digestive systems — they digest the world externally and absorb the result, which is why they own decomposition and why the same chemistry makes them both penicillin factory and crop destroyer.
